title: Proving a Client's Identity to an Authorization Server

questions.question: An MCP client is about to connect to a server whose authorization server it has never used before, and the client already has information on file for that authorization server. Per the specification's registration priority order, what should the client do?
options: Register a brand new client through Dynamic Client Registration to avoid using stale credentials
Use the pre-registered credentials it already has on file for that authorization server
Prompt the person to type in a client id before any request is sent to the server
Fetch a Client ID Metadata Document anyway, since that path is always preferred over stored information
questions.explanation: Pre-registered credentials come first in the priority order; a client only turns to Client ID Metadata Documents, then Dynamic Client Registration, then the user, when nothing is already on file for that issuer.

questions.question: A Client ID Metadata Document is fetched from https://app.example.com/oauth/client.json. Which property must the authorization server confirm before it trusts the document?
options: The document was fetched over plain HTTP so the authorization server can cache it
The document was registered ahead of time through a registration_endpoint call
The document's client_id field matches that URL exactly, character for character
The document includes a client secret the authorization server can verify locally
questions.explanation: The authorization server must validate that the client_id inside the fetched document equals the URL it was fetched from exactly; a mismatch means the document cannot be trusted as that client's identity.

questions.question: A desktop CLI tool registers through Dynamic Client Registration and redirects to http://127.0.0.1:PORT/callback. Which application_type should it declare?
options: confidential, because a CLI tool can store a client secret safely on local disk
It should omit application_type, since non-OIDC servers always ignore that field
web, because the authorization server only reads application_type for browser clients
native, because the tool is a locally hosted application reached through localhost
questions.explanation: Native applications, including desktop tools, CLIs, and locally hosted apps reached through localhost, should declare application_type native; omitting it defaults to web under OIDC and can conflict with a localhost redirect URI.

questions.question: A client's persisted credentials were issued by authorization server A. The protected resource metadata for the same MCP server now names authorization server B instead. What must the client do?
options: Treat the credentials as invalid for B, and register again with the correct server
Merge both authorization servers into one trust domain sharing a single client id
Forward the credentials from A to B and let B decide whether to accept them
Keep using the credentials from A, since the resource server itself has not changed
questions.explanation: Credentials are bound to the issuer that issued them; when the authorization server changes, the client must not reuse the old credentials and must re-register with the new one.

questions.question: An MCP proxy uses one static client id to reach a third-party authorization server on behalf of many dynamically registered downstream clients. What does the specification require of that proxy?
options: Nothing extra, because the static client id already represents every downstream client
It must obtain the user's consent for each dynamically registered client before forwarding
It must disable Dynamic Client Registration entirely for every downstream client it serves
It must rotate the static client id every single time a new downstream client appears
questions.explanation: A proxy using a static client id is a confused deputy risk; the specification requires it to obtain user consent for each dynamically registered client before forwarding that client's request to the third-party authorization server.

questions.question: A CI pipeline needs to call an MCP server on a nightly schedule with no person available to approve access. Which mechanism fits, and how must the server learn the client supports it?
options: Dynamic Client Registration, because it is the only flow built for an unattended client
Enterprise-Managed Authorization, since it removes the need for any access token entirely
The OAuth Client Credentials extension, declared in the client's per-request capabilities
The standard interactive authorization code flow, approved once in advance by an administrator
questions.explanation: Machine-to-machine access without an interactive user fits the OAuth Client Credentials extension, which a client declares in io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities.extensions on each request; extensions are opt-in and never active by default.
